summary: Defines the spamtest and virustest extensions for the Sieve mail filtering language. They give users simple, portable tests that match against numeric scores, while the underlying Sieve implementation does the real checking. It is a proposed standard that has been replaced by RFC 5235.

eli5.summary: Email filters can sort mail into folders. This adds a simple way to say, throw away anything the scanner scores as very spammy or virus-like. RFC 5235 replaced it.

questions: how to filter spam with sieve
subtitle: Portable spam and virus scoring tests for email filters.

tldr.problem: Every spam and virus scanning tool uses its own format to report results, making email filter scripts fragile and specific to particular tools.
tldr.mechanism: The spamtest and virustest extensions provide standardized numeric scores (0-10 for spam, 0-5 for viruses) that filter implementations map from whatever tools they use underneath.
tldr.outcome: Email users can write portable Sieve filters that work across different server implementations without depending on the specific scanner tool. RFC 5235 replaced it with an updated version.

today: RFC 5235 updated this specification in January 2008 with the same extensions, so this document is no longer current.

sections.title: Introduction and Overview
sections.content:
The SIEVE language is used by email servers to let users write rules that filter their mail. Before these extensions, many organizations used SIEVE with external spam and virus scanning tools, but every scanner tool reported results differently: some added headers with special syntax, some used codes only they understood. Users had to write custom filters for each tool, and when the tool changed or the server switched to a different scanner, the filters would break.

The spamtest and virustest extensions solve this by letting the server itself expose standardized numeric scores. The Sieve implementation can check mail with whatever scanners it uses, then report a simple number: for spam, a value from 0 to 10; for viruses, a value from 0 to 5. Users write rules that compare these numbers, and their scripts work on any compliant server.
sections.eli5: Email servers use tools to check for spam and viruses, but each tool reports its findings differently. These extensions give a standard way to ask the server for a number from 0 to 10 for spam or 0 to 5 for viruses.

sections.title: How the Tests Work
sections.content:
Both tests return a string that starts with a numeric value, optionally followed by a space and additional text. The string is compared using the SIEVE relational extension with the i;ascii-numeric comparator, which extracts just the numeric part at the beginning and ignores the rest. This lets implementations include extra details or reasons for the score without breaking the user's script.

Comparisons use SIEVE's standard match types like :is (equal), :ge (greater than or equal), and :lt (less than). The examples in the RFC use the relational extension to compare spam or virus scores numerically, allowing users to write rules like if spamtest :value "ge" "3" { fileinto "spam"; }.
sections.eli5: The server reports a number: the higher the number, the more likely the mail is spam or infected. Your filter can say, if the number is 5 or higher, move it to the spam folder.

sections.title: Spamtest Scores
sections.content:
The spamtest test evaluates to true when the spam score matches a value using the specified comparison. The score is a numeric value from 0 to 10 with the following meanings:

  • 0: message was not tested for spam (no scanner ran on it)
  • 1: message was tested and is clear of spam
  • 2-9: message was tested and has varying likelihood of containing spam, with higher numbers indicating higher likelihood
  • 10: message was tested and definitely contains spam

The server implementation maps the actual results from its spam detection tools into this standard range. For example, if a spam detector returns a confidence percentage, the implementation might scale it to fit this 0-10 scale.
sections.eli5: The spam score goes from 0 (definitely not spam) to 10 (definitely spam). The server figures out where to put mail from its own spam tools.

sections.title: Virus Scores and Security
sections.content:
The virustest test works similarly, with a numeric value from 0 to 5:

  • 0: message was not tested for viruses
  • 1: message was tested and contains no known viruses
  • 2: message was tested and contained a known virus which was replaced with harmless content
  • 3: message was tested and contained a known virus which was cured so it is now harmless
  • 4: message was tested and possibly contains a known virus
  • 5: message was tested and definitely contains a known virus

One critical security concern: if the implementation relies on headers added by scanners, it must ensure users cannot forge these headers to trick the filter into giving a false score. Administrators must also keep virus scanning tools up to date. However, the tests do not provide 100% virus protection, so users should still exercise caution with unknown senders.
sections.eli5: Virus scores go from 0 (no viruses) to 5 (definitely infected). But remember: no scanner catches everything, so stay careful with suspicious emails.

sections.title: Filtering with Scores
sections.content:
The RFC provides examples of how to use these tests. In one example, a filter sorts messages into different mailboxes based on their spam score: messages that were not scanned go to "INBOX.unclassified", and messages with a spamtest value of 3 or higher go to "INBOX.spam-trap". Another example quarantines messages with a virustest value of 4 and discards messages with a value of 5.

Because the scores are standard across implementations, users can move their filter scripts between different email servers without modification. The server is responsible for mapping its underlying tools to the standard numeric ranges, so the script remains portable.
sections.eli5: You write a filter that says: if spam score is 3 or more, move to the spam folder. If virus score is 5, delete it. Your filter works the same on any email server.
